subject: history
title: From Herodotus to Ranke
welcome_lead: How history became a discipline, from Greek inquiry to nineteenth-century professionalisation.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on the development of historical writing from antiquity to the nineteenth century.
final_note: You have walked among the founders of the craft.

concepts.def: Fifth-century BC Greek historian whose Histories investigated the Greco-Persian Wars; called the 'father of history'.
Athenian historian (c. 460-400 BC) of the Peloponnesian War, emphasising eyewitness evidence and political analysis.
Roman senatorial historian Tacitus (c. AD 56-120); also French Annales School later (founded 1929).
Tradition presenting the past as progress toward liberty and constitutional government, critiqued by Herbert Butterfield in 1931.
German historian (1795-1886) demanding source criticism and writing 'as it actually happened' (wie es eigentlich gewesen).
Approach treating each era on its own terms, seeking to understand context rather than judging by present standards.

walkthroughs.body_html: Herodotus's Histories combined ethnography, geography and oral testimony. Thucydides demanded eyewitness accounts and rejected divine causation. Roman historians like Livy and Tacitus shaped imperial narratives. Medieval chroniclers including Bede (Ecclesiastical History c. 731) integrated providential frameworks. Renaissance humanists rediscovered classical models, while Lorenzo Valla exposed the Donation of Constantine as a forgery in 1440.

Ranke established history as a university discipline in Berlin from 1825, training students through seminars to interrogate primary sources, especially diplomatic archives. His maxim 'wie es eigentlich gewesen' demanded objectivity. Critics argue Ranke privileged state archives and great-power diplomacy, marginalising social and economic history. Nonetheless, source criticism remains the methodological foundation of the discipline.

Herbert Butterfield's Whig Interpretation of History (1931) attacked historians who read the past as a triumphal march toward modern liberalism. Butterfield warned against anachronism and judging seventeenth-century figures by Victorian standards. The book reshaped how historians approached early modern England, encouraging contextual readings of Stuart politics. Butterfield himself later returned to providentialist themes in Christianity and History (1949).
